items.text: In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2.
items.why: Acknowledges architectural trade-off of reduced effective resolution.
items.plain: The Transformer makes relating positions require a constant number of operations, but this reduces effective resolution through averaging attention weights, which multi-head attention attempts to fix.

items.text: While for small values of dk the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk [3].
items.why: Highlights baseline comparison where additive attention beats unscaled dot product.
items.plain: Additive attention works better than unscaled dot-product attention when the key dimension is large.

items.text: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients 4.
items.why: States an unverified hypothesis for why scaling is necessary.
items.plain: The authors guess that large key dimensions make dot products grow large, pushing the softmax function into areas with tiny gradients.

items.text: Table 1: Maximum path lengths, per-layer complexity and minimum number of sequential operations for different layer types. n is the sequence length, d is the representation dimension, k is the kernel size of convolutions and r the size of the neighborhood in restricted self-attention.
items.why: Presents core theoretical complexity comparisons across layer types.
items.plain: A summary table comparing per-layer computational complexity, sequential operations, and maximum path length across self-attention, recurrent, and convolutional layers.

items.text: We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E)).
items.why: Reports ablation result comparing sinusoidal and learned positional embeddings.
items.plain: Using learned positional embeddings instead of sinusoidal ones gave almost identical results.

items.text: We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.
items.why: Claims structural advantage for extrapolation without empirical validation.
items.plain: The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings because they guess it might let the model handle sequences longer than those seen during training.

items.text: In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence
items.why: Limits the theoretical speed advantage to specific sequence lengths.
items.plain: Self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers only when the sequence length is smaller than the vector representation dimension.

items.text: This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.
items.why: Notes regularizer trade-off between perplexity and accuracy/BLEU.
items.plain: Label smoothing worsens training perplexity because the model becomes less certain, but it improves translation accuracy and BLEU scores.

items.text: The Transformer (big) model trained for English-to-French used dropout rate Pdrop = 0.1, instead of 0.3.
items.why: Reveals task-specific hyperparameter tuning for the primary model.
items.plain: The big model trained on English-to-French used a lower dropout rate of 0.1 instead of 0.3.

items.text: For the base models, we used a single model obtained by averaging the last 5 checkpoints, which were written at 10-minute intervals.
items.why: Details evaluation technique of checkpoint averaging that affects performance.
items.plain: For base models, the reported results come from averaging the last 5 saved training checkpoints.

items.text: For the big models, we averaged the last 20 checkpoints.
items.why: Details evaluation technique of averaging 20 checkpoints for big models.
items.plain: For big models, the final reported model was created by averaging the last 20 saved checkpoints.

items.text: These hyperparameters were chosen after experimentation on the development set.
items.why: Notes that generation hyperparameters were selected on the dev set.
items.plain: Beam search size and length penalty hyperparameters were picked based on experiments on the development dataset.

items.text: We estimate the number of floating point operations used to train a model by multiplying the training time, the number of GPUs used, and an estimate of the sustained single-precision floating-point capacity of each GPU 5.
items.why: Explains an indirect estimation method for training FLOPs.
items.plain: Training floating-point operations were estimated by multiplying run time, GPU count, and estimated hardware peak capacity.

items.text: We used beam search as described in the previous section, but no checkpoint averaging.
items.why: Notes evaluation difference between ablation table and main results.
items.plain: In the ablation variations table, the authors used beam search but did not average checkpoints.

items.text: While single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, quality also drops off with too many heads.
items.why: Reports ablation result showing optimal range for head counts.
items.plain: Using a single attention head lowers BLEU score by 0.9 compared to the best setting, but using too many heads also reduces translation quality.

items.text: In Table 3 rows (B), we observe that reducing the attention key size dk hurts model quality.
items.why: Reports ablation result when reducing key dimension size.
items.plain: Shrinking the attention key size hurts translation quality.

items.text: We performed only a small number of experiments to select the dropout, both attention and residual (section 5.4), learning rates and beam size on the Section 22 development set, all other parameters remained unchanged from the English-to-German base translation model.
items.why: Outlines parsing experiment setup and hyperparameter adjustments.
items.plain: Only a few hyperparameters like dropout, learning rates, and beam size were adjusted on the development set, while other settings remained identical to the translation model.
